## Motivation

Every year, millions of New Yorkers eat at restaurants without knowing whether the
kitchen passed its last health inspection, or whether neighbors have been filing
complaints about it for months. New York City's 311 system receives thousands of
food-related complaints annually, covering everything from rodent sightings to food
poisoning reports. At the same time, the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene
(DOHMH) conducts tens of thousands of restaurant inspections each year, assigning
letter grades and recording critical violations.

These two systems have largely been studied in isolation. Our project asks a simple
but consequential question:

> **Do neighborhoods with higher complaint activity experience systematically worse
> restaurant inspection outcomes?**

If the answer is yes, 311 complaints could serve as an early warning system: a cheap,
real-time signal that regulators could use to prioritize inspections before food safety
conditions deteriorate further. If complaints also trigger faster inspections, that
would suggest the system is already working in this direction, even if informally.

This question matters for three reasons. First, public health: identifying which
neighborhoods are at greatest food safety risk allows regulators to target enforcement
resources where they are most needed. Second, regulatory efficiency: the DOHMH
conducts inspections on a scheduled cycle, but complaint data could allow for smarter,
risk-based scheduling without additional cost. Third, equity: if lower-income
neighborhoods generate fewer complaints due to reporting barriers, they may receive
less inspection attention despite facing comparable or worse food safety conditions,
representing a compounding of inequality that warrants attention.

Prior research has examined restaurant inspection systems and established that grades
and violation rates are meaningful predictors of foodborne illness risk (Filion and
Powell, 2009; CDC, 2023). Scholarship on 311 data has shown that complaint volume
reflects both genuine neighborhood conditions and socioeconomic reporting patterns,
with higher-income and more digitally connected communities tending to over-report
relative to lower-income areas (O'Brien, 2015; Kontokosta and Hong, 2021). A 2019
report by the NYC Food Policy Center at Hunter College documented disparities in
restaurant grading across income and race lines in New York City specifically, but
did not leverage 311 complaint data as a predictive signal. Our work fills this gap
by combining DOHMH inspection data, 311 complaint data, and demographic context to
test whether complaints predict inspection outcomes and whether they accelerate
regulatory response. This specific combination, tested in post-COVID New York using
2022 to 2026 data, has not been previously published.

---

## Data

We draw on three publicly available datasets from NYC Open Data, covering the period
January 2022 through April 2026.

**DOHMH Restaurant Inspection Results** is our primary outcome dataset. It contains
285,460 inspection records across all five boroughs, including inspection dates,
violation codes, critical flags, scores, and letter grades. Each record represents
a single violation cited during an inspection visit. The data is comprehensive and
updated regularly, though inspection frequency varies by restaurant risk tier, which
introduces some unevenness in coverage across neighborhoods.

**311 Service Requests** is our primary predictor. We filtered the full 311 dataset
to food-relevant complaint types: Food Establishment, Food Poisoning, Rodent, and
Unsanitary Condition. This yielded 225,190 complaints over the study period. A key
limitation is reporting bias: higher-income, more digitally connected neighborhoods
may over-report relative to lower-income areas, meaning raw complaint volume reflects
both underlying risk and willingness to report.

**ACS Demographic Profiles** provided neighborhood-level population and income data
from the American Community Survey, used as contextual background for interpreting
borough-level differences in inspection outcomes.

We aggregated both primary datasets to the ZIP code level, matching complaints and
inspections by ZIP code and month to construct a panel dataset of 8,530 ZIP-month
observations. Geographic alignment between complaint ZIP codes and inspection
restaurant addresses introduces some measurement noise, which we treat as a
conservative bias in our estimates.

For full technical details on data acquisition, cleaning, and analysis, see the
individual reports linked at the end of this document.

---

## Findings

### Neighborhoods with More Complaints Have More Persistent Violations

Our first analysis asked whether neighborhoods that sustain high complaint volumes
over time also accumulate more repeat critical violations: cases where the same
restaurant is cited for the same violation on two or more separate inspection dates.
This is a particularly meaningful outcome because it signals entrenched, unresolved
non-compliance rather than a one-time lapse.

ZIP codes were grouped into four quartiles based on their average monthly complaint
volume. The lowest-complaint quartile (Q1) averaged 0.94 repeat critical violations
per restaurant, while the highest-complaint quartile (Q4) averaged 1.11, an 18%
difference. The mid-range Q3 neighborhoods peaked highest at 1.21, suggesting the
relationship is not perfectly linear. A statistical test comparing Q1 and Q4
produced a p-value of 0.063, just short of conventional significance, but the
directional trend is consistent and practically meaningful.

![Higher-Complaint Neighborhoods Have More Repeat Critical Violations. Avg repeat critical violations per restaurant by complaint quartile, with error bars showing variability within each group. Sources: DOHMH Inspections, NYC 311 (2022-2026).](figures/sq1_plot.png)

### Higher Complaint Volume Predicts Worse Inspection Scores

The second analysis took a broader view, asking whether overall inspection performance
is worse in neighborhoods that generate more food-related complaints. Using a
regression model that controlled for borough-level differences in restaurant density
and demographics, we found that each doubling of complaint volume is associated with
a 1.08-point increase in average inspection score. Since higher scores mean worse
outcomes in the DOHMH system, this confirms that more-complained-about ZIP codes
genuinely perform worse when inspectors arrive. The model explains 34% of the
variation in inspection scores across ZIP codes, a substantial share for a
neighborhood-level analysis.

Brooklyn and Queens show significantly worse inspection outcomes than the Bronx
baseline even after controlling for complaint volume. Manhattan, despite having the
highest raw complaint numbers of any borough, does not differ significantly from the
Bronx once restaurant density is accounted for. This suggests that Manhattan's high
complaint totals largely reflect its extraordinary concentration of restaurants rather
than systematically worse food safety conditions.

![More Complaints, Higher (Worse) Inspection Scores. Each point represents one ZIP code. The dashed line shows the overall positive trend. Color indicates borough. Sources: DOHMH Inspections, NYC 311 (2022-2026).](figures/sq2_scatter.png)

### Complaints and Violations Reflect the Same Conditions, Not a Causal Chain

The third analysis tested whether complaint spikes actually predict future inspection
deterioration, or whether complaints and violations simply co-occur because they both
reflect the same persistent neighborhood conditions. We examined whether complaint
volume in one month predicts inspection outcomes in the following one, two, and three
months.

The lagged correlations are consistently positive but very small, ranging from 0.03
to 0.08, and none reached statistical significance after controlling for stable
neighborhood characteristics. This is an important and honest null finding. It tells
us that the complaint-inspection relationship is contemporaneous rather than
predictive: neighborhoods with chronic food safety challenges generate both complaints
and violations in the same period, rather than complaints accumulating ahead of a
future wave of violations. This means 311 data is most useful as a concurrent
diagnostic of neighborhood risk rather than as a pure early warning system.

### Food Establishment Complaints Are the Strongest Signal

Not all complaint types are equally informative. The fourth analysis examined which
of the four complaint categories shows the strongest association with critical
violation rates at the ZIP code level.

Contrary to the initial hypothesis that rodent complaints would be most predictive,
Food Establishment complaints showed the strongest correlation with critical violations
(r = 0.157), followed by Rodent (r = 0.116), Food Poisoning (r = 0.109), and
Unsanitary Condition (r = 0.047). All four types point in the same direction. The
stronger performance of Food Establishment complaints likely reflects the breadth of
the category: it captures a wide range of concerns about restaurant conditions, from
visible cleanliness to food handling practices, making it a more comprehensive signal
about overall restaurant quality than any single specific complaint type.

From a policy perspective, this finding suggests that Food Establishment complaints
may be the most useful signal for risk-based inspection targeting, despite being less
intuitively associated with critical violations than rodent sightings.

### Complaints Dramatically Accelerate Inspection Timelines

The fifth and most striking finding concerns the speed of regulatory response. We
matched each food-related 311 complaint to the next inspection occurring in the same
ZIP code within 180 days, then compared the resulting time-to-inspection against the
baseline gap between consecutive inspections.

The baseline median gap between inspections is 315 days, roughly ten months. The
median time from a food-related 311 complaint to the next inspection in the same
ZIP code is just 4 days, 311 days faster. A statistical test confirms this difference
is overwhelmingly significant. Food Poisoning complaints triggered the fastest
response at a median of 3 days, while Rodent complaints were slightly slower at 5
days. Across all complaint types, more than 90% of matched inspections occurred
within 30 days of the complaint.

This finding should be interpreted with care. Our ZIP-level matching means some of
these inspections may be routine visits to nearby restaurants rather than direct
responses to the specific complaint. Even so, the magnitude of the difference is too
large to be explained by coincidence. The 311 system appears to be functioning as a
genuine accelerant for regulatory action, translating citizen concern into measurably
faster government response.

---

## Overall Answer to the Overarching Question

Taken together, our five analyses paint a consistent picture: yes, neighborhoods with
higher complaint activity do experience systematically worse restaurant inspection
outcomes.

High-complaint ZIP codes show more repeat critical violations (Analysis 1), higher
inspection scores (Analysis 2), and worse grades across all complaint types
(Analysis 4). The relationship is contemporaneous rather than predictive (Analysis 3),
suggesting complaints and violations reflect shared underlying conditions rather than
a simple causal chain. Most encouragingly, the regulatory system appears responsive:
complaints are associated with dramatically faster subsequent inspections (Analysis 5),
suggesting 311 already functions as an informal but effective prioritization mechanism.

The quantitative story is coherent. A one-unit increase in log complaint volume
predicts a 1.08-point worsening in inspection score. Q4 neighborhoods show 18% more
repeat critical violations than Q1. Post-complaint inspections arrive 311 days faster
than the baseline cycle. These are not small or ambiguous effects: they represent
real, measurable differences in food safety outcomes and regulatory responsiveness
across New York City neighborhoods.

**Limitations.** Our ZIP-level analysis cannot establish causality. Reporting bias
in 311 data likely understates complaint volume in lower-income areas. The Analysis 5
matching is conservative, using ZIP rather than restaurant address, meaning the true
complaint-to-inspection effect is likely stronger than measured. The study window
(2022-2026) may not capture longer-term trends.

---

## Prior Work and Novelty

Our project builds on three bodies of existing work. Research on restaurant inspection
systems has established that grades and violation rates are meaningful predictors of
foodborne illness risk (Filion and Powell, 2009; CDC, 2023). Scholarship on 311 data
has shown that complaint volume reflects both genuine neighborhood conditions and
socioeconomic reporting patterns (O'Brien, 2015; Kontokosta and Hong, 2021). The NYC
Food Policy Center (2019) documented disparities in restaurant grading across income
and race lines in New York City specifically.

Our contribution is to link these streams directly: combining DOHMH inspection data,
311 complaint data, and demographic context to test whether complaints predict
inspection outcomes and whether they accelerate regulatory response. This specific
combination, tested in post-COVID New York using 2022-2026 data, has not been
previously published. Prior work examined inspections and complaints separately;
we test whether they are connected, how strongly, and through what mechanisms.

---

## Future Work

Several extensions would strengthen and deepen this analysis.

**Restaurant-level matching.** Our ZIP-level approach is conservative. Matching
complaints to specific restaurants by address would allow a cleaner test of whether
complaints trigger inspections at the establishment level, removing the noise
introduced by geographic aggregation.

**Incorporating Yelp and Google reviews.** Online reviews represent a third signal
of food safety concern not filtered through the 311 system. Combining citizen
complaints, online reviews, and inspection outcomes could substantially improve
predictive power.

**Socioeconomic moderation.** A fuller analysis would test whether the
complaint-to-inspection relationship differs by neighborhood income level,
specifically whether lower-income areas receive slower regulatory responses for the
same complaint volume. This would surface a potential equity concern that our
current analysis can only gesture toward.

**Pre- vs post-COVID comparison.** Our data begins in 2022. Comparing pre- and
post-COVID inspection patterns would reveal whether the pandemic disrupted the
complaint-inspection relationship and whether it has since recovered.
